_readme: What's new, written for the person using Retake — not for whoever wrote it. Both the landing page and the Retake window read THIS file; there is no second copy. Rules for adding one: say what changed for them, name no files, no flags they will not type, no words like refactor or regression. If a line only makes sense to someone who has read the source, it does not belong here. Newest first. Add an entry on every release that changes what people see.

releases.headline: The extra checks are optional, and nothing pretends otherwise
notes: Recording a demo is the whole job. The checks that look at how it came out are extras you run against a recording you already have, and a few places had started to word that as though a demo were unfinished without them. It isn't, and now nothing says so.
In the window, the row of checks is labelled — it reads as things you can run, not as things that are missing.
Retake still recommends looking at the frames before telling somebody an app works. That is about the claim, not about the recording.

releases.headline: Retake now knows what your product is for — and says how it knows
notes: New: tell Retake what your product is, who uses it, and what about it is deliberate. Every visual check reads it. Until now they judged your app as a generic web page, which means anything you did on purpose could come back as a mistake.

This is measured, not claimed. On a real charter console a line that is set faint on purpose — an internal note the desk is meant to see quietly — was reported as a contrast problem. With one paragraph explaining the screen, that complaint disappeared and a genuine one took its place: a developer link left visible on a page a customer sees. The same number of findings, better findings.

New: every finding now says how it was arrived at. Something that was performed reads differently from something visible in a picture, which reads differently again from something read in the code and never run. You can tell at a glance which findings somebody watched happen and which are somebody's reasoning.

This is the difference between a report you can act on and one you have to re-check yourself — and it is the failure that made this worth building: a review can be technically careful and still be wrong about the product, because it never used it.
Both are optional. Say nothing and everything works exactly as before.

releases.headline: You can see what it is doing — and the window is no longer open to the internet
notes: New: the window shows what is happening while it happens. Which demo, which phase — putting the app in a known state, opening the browser, recording, rendering, checking — a progress bar, the step it is on, and how long it has been going. It works whether an agent started the recording or you typed the command yourself, because the run writes it down rather than having to tell anyone.

Security: the window had no lock on its door. Any website you happened to have open could tell it to run any command on your machine. It now needs a key that only programs on your own computer can read, refuses anything coming from another site, and no longer takes a command from whoever asked — it looks up your project's own start script instead.

New: record a demo without waiting for its pauses. All the steps, none of the holding still. On a real demo that is 81 seconds instead of 156. It is for while you are working — Retake marks it and refuses to call it finished, so it can never be handed over by mistake.

Fixed: installing Retake fresh was broken. The starter demo it promised to create was missing from the package, so a new workspace came out incomplete. It is there now, and there is a test that installs into an empty folder and checks.
Fixed: a half-finished recording could be reported as ready to ship.

releases.headline: Record a demo without waiting for its pauses
notes: A demo that is nice to watch spends a lot of its time holding still — a beat after a click so you can see what happened, a moment on the result before moving on. On one real recording that was 317 of 509 seconds. Sixty-two per cent of the take was pausing.
That pacing is exactly right for the video somebody watches, and pure waiting while you are still changing the demo. Until now there was no way to have one without the other.

New: record the whole thing without the pacing. Every pause skipped, every wait shortened. All the steps still run and all of them are still in the video — only the holding still is gone. On that same demo it is three and a half minutes instead of eight and a half.

It is for while you are working, not for the video you keep. Retake marks the recording so it can never be mistaken for the finished one, and so nothing quietly hands it back to you later as if it were.

releases.headline: Checking a demo again is nearly free — and looking twice finds more
notes: Checking every frame of a demo used to cost a minute or so every time, even when nothing had changed. Now an answer is kept against the frame itself, so re-checking a demo you have not re-recorded takes about a second. Change one screen and only that screen is looked at again.

And a thing worth knowing, because it was measured rather than assumed: looking once is not reliable. On a frame with a genuine problem on it, three checks in a row walked past it and a fourth caught it.

So looking again now adds to what is already known instead of replacing it. Two extra passes over a real recording took it from nine frames with something on them to eleven — including the one that mattered. Because repeat passes are nearly free, that is now the sensible thing to do on any screen you care about.
None of it is stored anywhere you have to manage, and none of it runs while you are recording.

releases.headline: The checks are four times faster, and they say what they saw
notes: Checking a demo used to run one question at a time. On a demo with thirty-four things written on it that was six minutes — long enough that an agent skips it, which makes a check worthless however good it is. It is a minute and a half now.

Every answer now says what it actually saw before it gives a verdict, not just yes or no. That is how you catch a wrong answer: when the description does not match the picture, you know not to trust the verdict.

releases.headline: See at a glance whether anyone actually checked a demo
notes: New: one quiet line under each recording showing what has been checked on it — the questions written on its scenes, every frame swept for the ten ways a picture goes wrong, whether the numbers add up, and anything you flagged. With a dash where nothing has run.
It is about the recording that is there now. Re-record a demo and every earlier answer is shown as answering an older take, because it is.
This closes a real gap: an agent could tell you it checked something and there was no way to know. Now there is — the checks write it down when they run, and the window reads it back.
And Retake will tell you which demos nobody has looked at. Run the one-line summary of your whole workspace and it names them.

releases.headline: The flagging feature your agents could not see
notes: Fixed: everything to do with flagging — saying something is really wrong, and checking later whether it got fixed — existed only as a terminal command. Your agents drive Retake through a different door and had no way to reach it, and no document mentioned it. So a whole feature shipped that nobody could use. It is reachable now, and written into the instructions agents read.
Fixed: when an agent ran the picture check, anything you had flagged was quietly skipped — and it still reported a pass. It now answers those too.
Retake now fails its own build if a new feature is not reachable from every place it should be. A promise to remember was not going to hold.

releases.headline: Retake looks at every frame the way a stranger would
notes: New: one command goes through every single frame of a demo and tells you what looks wrong on it — text cut off or spilling out of its box, things sitting on top of each other, writing you can't read against its background, something running off the edge, an element drawn twice, a spinner still spinning, a broken image, a developer badge left in shot, a blank space where something belongs.

This finds what nobody thought to ask about. The other checks answer questions you wrote down, which means they can only ever find what you already suspected — the same reason you can stare at a screen, checking whether the thing you just fixed is fixed, and walk straight past something else that is plainly broken. That happened here, and this is the answer to it.
It proved itself on the first real recording it was pointed at: three labels with the card below sitting on top of them, on a screen a person had already looked at directly and passed.
Every frame, never a sample. Sampling is how the looking goes wrong in the first place.
It reports rather than fails. Some of what it finds is correct and unimportant — it says what it can see, names the frame, and leaves the call to you.

releases.headline: Check the things you flagged without watching the whole demo again
notes: New: when something is wrong in a demo, say so once and Retake watches it from then on. Every recording after that answers it — and shows you the few seconds of video that prove it, instead of asking you to sit through the whole thing again. On a five-minute walkthrough that is about twenty seconds instead of five minutes.
The clips are cut from the video you already have. Nothing is re-recorded and nothing is re-rendered.

In the window: a quiet line above the frames — "2 things you flagged here. 1 now passes." Click either one to watch just that moment, and one button puts the whole demo back. It only appears when you have actually flagged something.
Flagging never edits your demo file. It is kept in a small list beside it, so the file you wrote stays exactly as you wrote it.

Fixed: recordings that were invisible. The window used to list demos, and show each demo's recording — so if the file a demo came from went missing, a perfectly good video simply never appeared. Eight of them were sitting on this machine, including a five-minute one. They show up now, and there is a one-line way to put the missing files back.
None of this happens while you are recording. It cannot slow a take down, and there is a test that proves the recorder cannot even reach it.

releases.headline: Retake checks whether your app makes sense — and goes looking for what you didn't think of
notes: New: Retake can tell you when a flow doesn't add up. It reads everything a demo typed, chose and clicked, puts that against the pictures it took, and asks about the parts that don't agree. It found a real one the first time it ran: a charter quote where two flights were entered and one price was shown. Every step had passed. Every frame looked fine. The recording had known for weeks.
It asks rather than accuses. Whether a number adds up is a judgement call, so what comes back is questions you settle in a couple of seconds — not a red X that stops everything.

New: a way to find what you didn't think of. Point it at a demo you already have and it writes out a whole set of new ones — the same flow but with the button pressed twice, the page reloaded halfway, the thing it depends on switched off, nothing in the app yet, 540 characters typed into every box, quotes and emoji everywhere, nothing waiting for anything. Then it tries them all.
What comes back is files, not a report. Every one of them is a normal demo you can read, run again, keep, or throw away — so if it finds something, you already have the recipe for it.

It knows the difference between your app breaking and your app defending itself. A second press that finds nothing means the button went away, which is your app doing the right thing — it says so instead of crying wolf. And when something is genuinely a judgement call, it says that too rather than guessing.

It refuses to touch anything that isn't running on your own machine, anything whose data it can't put back, and anything somebody else is recording at that moment. Each of those can be overruled, but only by you and only on purpose.
Under the hood: the checks now live apart from the recorder, so none of them can affect a recording, and any of them could be removed tomorrow without the rest noticing.

releases.headline: Retake can now tell you whether your app actually looks right — and what keeps going wrong
notes: New: say what should be visible, and Retake checks it. On any scene you can write a plain sentence — "every card sits inside its own box", "the button's text is readable against its background" — and Retake puts that question to a second pair of eyes, against the actual frame it recorded. It answers yes or no, and tells you what it saw.

This is the check nothing else was doing. A page can pass every test, build clean, and still be broken in a way only a person notices: an animation frozen halfway, an icon that never loaded, a card that fell out of its grid, a label in dark text on a dark background. All four of those happened here in one day, and all four were caught by someone looking — not by anything the tools did. Now the tool looks.
The one judging it is never the one who made it. Retake asks a separate reader that sees only the picture and the question, so an agent cannot mark its own homework.

If it couldn't check, it says so rather than passing. No frame, nothing available to look at it, an answer it couldn't read — every one of those counts as a failure. A check that didn't run is not a check that passed.
Nothing changes unless you want it to. Demos without any of these sentences record exactly as before.

Also new: Retake reads your own recordings back to you. One command and it goes through every demo you have made and says the few things worth saying — a demo quietly showing live data when it was meant to show fake, the same button failing in five different demos because your app moved, a half-recording left sitting where the finished one should be, a demo nobody has ever checked the look of. It says nothing when there is nothing to say.
And when something it finds is really a habit rather than a one-off, it hands you a sentence to put in your agents' instructions — so the next agent does not repeat it.

releases.headline: You can see what your agent is doing, and it finishes what it started
notes: Captions are off by default now. A caption under the app makes you look away from the thing you came to watch, so a demo no longer paints them on unless you ask. Scene captions are still worth writing — they name the beats in the proof log and the stills.

Re-recording only what changed. Edit part of a demo you already recorded and Retake works out which scene your change starts at, then records from there instead of from the beginning. On a long demo that is a couple of minutes instead of eight.

Renders are much faster while you are still working on a demo. Skipping the archival copy took an eight-minute video from about eight minutes of encoding down to under three — and the video you hand over is very slightly better for it, because it is no longer a copy of a copy.

A progress bar while a demo records — how many steps in, how long it has been going, and roughly how long the render has left. The window used to just say "Recording…" and then nothing at all, sometimes for a quarter of an hour.
If your agent disconnects mid-recording, the recording now finishes and saves instead of dying halfway.
And if a recording is killed outright, it leaves a note saying which part it reached — so you can pick up from there instead of starting the whole thing again.
If a recording quietly stops making progress, the window says so — no step finished in 90 seconds — instead of leaving you guessing whether it is working or hung.
And if Retake gets updated while your agent is mid-session, it now tells the agent that it is running the older version and needs restarting, rather than silently missing the new behaviour.

releases.headline: Videos come out the size you asked for — and changing your mind is nearly free
notes: Every video is exactly the size of the format you picked. Landscape is 1920×1080, square is square, vertical fits a phone. No more sizes drifting between takes.
Changing your mind costs seconds, not another recording. Size, shape, format, captions, speed, zoom, music, title cards and the cover image all re-make themselves from the recording you already have.
Moved a caption to the wrong moment? Nudge it. The caption, the still and the cover all follow, and you never record again.

Only the ending changed? Record only the ending. The earlier steps still run so your app gets to the right place, but they happen at full speed and off camera. On a seven-minute demo that is about three minutes instead of sixteen.

Your old recordings are kept. A re-record no longer throws away the take you had — you can look at the previous ones and go back to any of them. Only the recording itself is stored, so it stays small.
A failed recording can no longer cost you the one that worked.
New: clear out old files safely. It shows you what it would free before removing anything, and never touches a recording.
In the window: pick several demos at once — or a whole folder — and archive them together. The archive empties in one click.
Launch videos can open with a title card and close with your own sign-off, put music underneath, and add a spoken voiceover.
Dead air gets trimmed: while your app is thinking, the video moves through the wait instead of sitting in it.
You can sign in to a demo account without any AI ever seeing your password.
Renders are about twice as fast.

Your agent now checks far more before recording — that a click will land on something clickable, that a stub is really being used, that it is looking at the same screen the recording will — so fewer takes are wasted finding out mid-recording.
On a long demo your agent shows you a quick draft and asks before spending the full recording.
The window has been rebuilt: one place for everything, and it stops shouting at you.

releases.headline: Demos behind a login
notes: Demos of apps that need signing in. You sign in once in a real browser window; nothing types your password and nothing records it.
The video player shows your video in its own shape, with no black bars around it.

releases.headline: The first public release
notes: Describe a demo in one readable file, and get a video, still frames, and a written record of what happened.
When your app changes, fix the file and run it again — instead of recording the whole thing over.
